2. Ciliary Body
-Ring-shaped thickened tissue between iris and choroid.
-Contains blood vessels, connective tissue, and ciliary muscle.
-Divided into:
- Pars plicata (anterior) -> aqueous humour secretion
- Pars plana (posterior)
Functions:
1 Accommodation
-Ciliary muscle contraction -> zonules relax -> lens becomes convex -> near focus
-Relaxation -> lens flattens -> distant focus
2 Aqueous humour production
3 Attachment for zonular fibers (lens support)

explanation_verbatim:
Intermediate Uveitis (Pars Planitis / Cyclitis)
Definition: Inflammation of vitreous & peripheral retina.
Age: 15–40 years (often bilateral, asymmetric).
Causes:
•Infectious: TB, Syphilis, Toxoplasmosis, Toxocariasis
•Non-infectious: Sarcoidosis, Multiple sclerosis
Symptoms:
•Floaters
•Blurred vision (insidious onset)
Signs:
•Vitreous cells & haziness
•Snowballs: white aggregates in inferior vitreous
•Snowbanking: grey-white plaques on pars plana
•May have anterior uveitis in 50%

stem:
Diagnostic Criteria (All required for diagnosis):
1.No history of penetrating ocular trauma or surgery.
2.No other ocular disease that explains the inflammation.
3.Bilateral granulomatous panuveitis.
4.Neurological and/or auditory manifestations:
- Headache (aseptic meningitis)
- Tinnitus
- Vertigo
- Hearing loss
5.Skin and hair involvement:
- Vitiligo (depigmented patches)
- Alopecia
- Poliosis (whitening of eyelashes or eyebrows)

explanation_verbatim:
Ocular Features:
•Bilateral granulomatous panuveitis
•Exudative retinal detachment
•Disc edema
•Mutton-fat keratic precipitates
Treatment:
1.Systemic corticosteroids (mainstay)
2.Immunosuppressive therapy in refractory cases (azathioprine, cyclosporine, etc.)
3.Topical corticosteroids + cycloplegics for ocular inflammation

Treatment:
•High-dose corticosteroids (systemic + topical)
•Immunosuppressive agents in severe or refractory cases
•Early enucleation of the injured eye (if vision is lost and inflammation severe) within 10-14 days may help prevent sympathetic involvement

stem: A 32-year-old male patient presented with diminution of vision, photophobia, ocular pain and redness in his right eye. Examination of the eye showed ciliary injection, anterior chamber cells, keratic precipitates and aqueous flare. Which of the following is a possible line of treatment?

A 32-year-old male patient presented with diminution of vision, photophobia, ocular pain and redness in his right eye. Examination of the eye showed ciliary injection, anterior chamber cells, keratic precipitates and aqueous flare. Which of the following is a possible line of treatment?
explanation_verbatim: Anterior uveitis (iridocyclitis) is treated with topical corticosteroids to reduce inflammation. Cycloplegic agents may also be added for pain relief.

stem: Which of the following is part of the uveal tract?
Which of the following is part of the uveal tract?
explanation_verbatim: The uveal tract consists of the iris, ciliary body, and choroid. These vascular layers provide nourishment and are involved in uveitis.

stem: A 28-year-old patient presents with sudden onset of unilateral eye redness, pain, and photophobia. Work-up reveals uveitis. Which systemic condition is most likely associated with this presentation?
A 28-year-old patient presents with sudden onset of unilateral eye redness, pain, and photophobia. Work-up reveals uveitis. Which systemic condition is most likely associated with this presentation?
explanation_verbatim: Anterior uveitis is commonly associated with HLA-B27 diseases such as ankylosing spondylitis. It presents with unilateral redness, pain, and photophobia.

stem: A 35-year-old patient presents with decreased vision, ocular pain, and a constricted pupil that reacts sluggishly to light. Slit-lamp examination confirms anterior uveitis. What is the first-line treatment for this condition?

A 35-year-old patient presents with decreased vision, ocular pain, and a constricted pupil that reacts sluggishly to light. Slit-lamp examination confirms anterior uveitis. What is the first-line treatment for this condition?
explanation_verbatim: Topical corticosteroids are the mainstay treatment for anterior uveitis to reduce inflammation. Cycloplegics may also be added to relieve pain and prevent synechiae.

stem: Which of the following is a cause of dilated fixed pupil?
Which of the following is a cause of dilated fixed pupil?
explanation_verbatim: Causes of dilated fixed pupil -> Trauma to the iris sphincter or the orbital parasympathetic nerves (traumatic mydriasis), Pharmacologic dilatation, Ciliary ganglion disease / damage, Oculomotor (III) Paralysis, Brain stem affection (dorsal midbrain syndrome), Stage III anaesthesia & Death (bilateral).

stem: Which of the following conditions is among the causes of secondary angle closure glaucoma?
Which of the following conditions is among the causes of secondary angle closure glaucoma?
explanation_verbatim: Causes of secondary angle closure glaucoma → Uveitis, neovascular glaucoma (PDR, CRVO) & phacomorphic glaucoma.

stem: What is the percentage of aqueous humor that is drained by the uveo-scleral pathway?
What is the percentage of aqueous humor that is drained by the uveo-scleral pathway?
explanation_verbatim: The trabecular pathway is responsible for 90% of the aqueous outflow from the eye. On the other hand, the uveoscleral pathway is responsible for 10% of the aqueous outflow from the eye.

stem: A 29-year-old man complains of eye pupil constriction, eyelid drooping and diminished unilateral sweating. Which of the following is the cause of that patient's condition?
A 29-year-old man complains of eye pupil constriction, eyelid drooping and diminished unilateral sweating. Which of the following is the cause of that patient's condition?
explanation_verbatim: Horner syndrome → It is caused by dysfunction of the sympathetic supply. It is characterized by Miosis (with anisocoria mere in the dark), Ptosis and anhidrosis of the ipsilateral face and neck, Enophthalmos & Heterochromia of the iris in congenital cases.

stem: A 35-year-old male patient presented with floaters and blurry vision. Examination revealed snow balls and small banking. What is the best line of treatment for such a patient?
A 35-year-old male patient presented with floaters and blurry vision. Examination revealed snow balls and small banking. What is the best line of treatment for such a patient?
explanation_verbatim:
Signs of intermediate uveitis → Snowballs (aggregates of inflammatory cells in the inferior vitreous) & Snow banking (grey-white fibrovascular plaques on the inferior pars plana).
Main treatment of uveitis → Steroids.

53 years old patient complaining of near vision problems. The patient is asthmatic and has some degree of heart block that is controlled medically. His visual acuity is 6/6 in both eyes. While examination you notice nuclear sclerosis in both eyes. IOP is 28 mmHg in his right eye and 30 mmHg in his left eye, the fundus examination revealed large cup/disc ratio in both eyes. Your diagnosis is POAG. You are going to prescribe medical treatment to him.
What are group of drugs that should be avoided in that patient?
explanation_verbatim: Topical beta-blockers like timolol can cause bronchospasm and worsen heart block, so they should be avoided. Other agents like prostaglandin analogues are preferred.
